extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, poets, and playwrights studying poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Aristotle's formative principles for poetry and dramatic art, including what poetry imitates (mimesis), how poetic species differ, the media they use (rhythm, language, tune), and what must be represented for a successful plot. Useful for informing composition, genre classification, and theoretical critique of poems and plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of poetry's essence, species, functions, and plot construction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us here deal with Poetry, its essence and its several species, with the characteristic function of each species and the way in which plots must be constructed if the poem is to be a success; and also with the number and character of the constituent parts of a poem...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry as an art with an essence and multiple species; success depends on proper construction of the plot and on the correct number and character of a poem's constituent parts. Begin analysis from first principles and attend to both overall form (plot) and elemental composition (parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as representation of life (μίμησις)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Epic poetry, then, and the poetry of tragic drama, and, moreover, comedy and dithyrambic poetry, and most flute-playing and harp-playing, these, speaking generally, may all be said to be 'representations of life.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimesis: the artist re-presents phenomena of sense in his medium, giving coherence and designing a pattern rather than merely copying. This principle applies across genres (epic, tragedy, comedy, music). Consider how a work shapes and orders life-events into a patterned representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold grounds of difference among poetic species
rubrics_metrics.description: “But they differ one from another in three ways: either in using means generically different or in representing different objects or in representing objects not in the same way but in a different manner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify genres by (1) their medium/means, (2) the objects they represent (types of life/events), or (3) the manner/style of representation. Use this triad to explain why two works are distinct genres or why a work belongs to a particular species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of representation: rhythm, language, and tune
rubrics_metrics.description: “For just as by the use both of color and form people represent many objects, making likenesses of them... so is it also in the arts which we have mentioned, they all make their representations in rhythm and language and tune, using these means either separately or in combination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating works, identify which of the three means (rhythm, language, tune) are employed and whether they operate singly or in combination. The choice of means shapes how life is represented and what can be conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific functions of tune and rhythm (music and dance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “For tune and rhythm alone are employed in flute-playing and harp-playing and in any other arts which have a similar function... Rhythm alone without tune is employed by dancers in their representations, for by means of rhythmical gestures they represent both character and experiences and actions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different media have formal affordances: instrumental music relies on tune and rhythm; dance relies on rhythm (gesture) to represent character and actions. Match formal choices to the aspects of life you want to represent; do not expect every medium to perform every representational task equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of words: bare prose versus metres
rubrics_metrics.description: “But the art which employs words either in bare prose or in metres,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between prose and metrical language as compositional means. The selection between prose and metre is a fundamental formal decision that affects how events, character, and emotion are represented and perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of representation: πράξεις (actions) and πάθη (experiences/tragic incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: “πάθη καὶ πράξεις cover the whole field of life, what men do (πρᾶξεις) and what men experience (πάθη). ... as a technical term in this treatise πάθος is a calamity or tragic incident, something that happens to the hero.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing, attend to both actions (what characters do) and experiences/emotional events (what happens to them). In tragedy, 'πάθος' specifically denotes calamities or tragic incidents affecting the hero; understanding these technical senses is crucial to applying Aristotle's framework.
